summary: Specifies how certificates in formats other than X.509v3 can be requested using PKIX certificate management protocols, using CRMF. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Most ID cards use the same shape, but sometimes you want a different shape. This memo shows how to ask for them using the same forms.

questions: how to request an openpgp certificate from a ca
what is a key template in cmp
subtitle: How to ask a PKIX certificate authority for attribute or OpenPGP certificates using the same request syntax as X.509.

tldr.problem: PKIX certificate management protocols focus on X.509v3 public-key certificates, but sometimes other certificate formats must be managed too.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines templates for X.509 attribute certificates and OpenPGP certificates that fit into the CRMF request syntax, and extends the CMP and CMC protocols so they can carry these certificates.
tldr.outcome: CMP and CMC can request and return attribute and OpenPGP certificates, with security caveats around request authorisation and PGP parsing. The IESG note says this is not a candidate for any Internet Standard.

today: RFC 4212 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The IESG note states it is not a candidate for any Internet Standard.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The PKIX working group has several certificate management protocols, mostly aimed at X.509v3 public-key certificates. This RFC focuses on the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF, RFC 4211), which is used by protocols such as PKIX-CMP (RFC 4210) and CMC (RFC 2797).

CMP had already defined a framework for alternative certificate templates, but not the exact formats. This document defines how CRMF can request two types: X.509 attribute certificates and OpenPGP certificates. It also extends CMP and CMC so they can return such certificates.

The IESG note says this document is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and the IETF disclaims any knowledge of its fitness for any purpose. It has not had IETF review for security, congestion control or interaction with deployed protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a request form for one kind of ID card. This memo adds boxes on the form for two other kinds of card.

sections.title: Certificate Templates
sections.content:
A CRMF CertTemplate lets a requester say as much or as little as it wants about the certificate it wants. The CA has the final say over the actual content. For other certificate types, CMP introduced the id-regCtrl-altCertTemplate control. It may be used only when the certTemplate is empty, and MUST NOT be used when the certTemplate has any field present.

For attribute certificates, the template is an AttCertTemplate under the OID id-acTemplate. Every field (version, holder, issuer, signature, serial number, validity, attributes, unique ID, extensions) is optional.

For OpenPGP, the template is an OpenPGPCertTemplateExtended that wraps an OpenPGP certificate in which all fields are optional. It is encoded as an ASN.1 OCTET STRING in binary form without Radix-64 conversion.
sections.plainLanguage: The request form has blanks. You fill in what you care about and leave the rest empty, and the issuer decides the final details.

sections.title: The OpenPGP Template Rules
sections.content:
Every packet in an OpenPGP CertTemplate MUST be a syntactically correct OpenPGP packet, so existing PGP libraries can build and parse them. Because enumerated fields cannot be left empty, the RFC defines special values that do not change the OpenPGP syntax:

  • A time field of zero means "any time".
  • A key ID of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF means "any key id".
  • A signature whose MPIs are all 0xFF is a Signature Template. It asks the CA to put a real certification signature there.
  • Key material in which at least one MPI is all 1 bits is a Key Template. It asks the CA or RA to generate the key pair.

If the template has no Public Key packet, it refers to any public key. If it has no User ID packets, it refers to any user IDs relevant to the request. If any requested certification signature cannot be granted, the whole request MUST be rejected.

With a Key Template, the CA or RA SHOULD also create a self-signature, and for subkeys a binding signature if it knows the primary private key. A conformant implementation is REQUIRED to support templates that are valid OpenPGP certificates, and to either support Key and Signature Templates or reject requests containing them.
sections.plainLanguage: Special placeholder values mean "anything is fine here" or "please make one for me". The issuer fills in those spots when it signs the final certificate.

sections.title: Proof of Possession and Protocol Changes
sections.content:
A CRMF request includes a Proof-of-Possession (POP) showing the requester holds the private key. If the template contains the subject and public key, the signature is computed over the DER-encoded request or the DER-encoded AltCertTemplate. An OpenPGP template meets this condition if it has a Public Key packet (not a Key Template) and at least one User ID packet.

In PKIX-CMP, the CMPCertificate choice is expanded with x509v2AttCert (tag 0) and openPGPCert (tag 2). In CMC, the CMS CertificateChoices gains openPGPCert (tag 3). CMC's rule that each CRMF message MUST include the subject and public key is extended to cover the altCertTemplate control.
sections.plainLanguage: You still have to prove you own the secret key. The certificate envelopes used by the two protocols get extra slots for the new kinds of certificates.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions inherit CRMF's security considerations. Request security relies on the protocol used to talk to the CA. Both CMP and CMC give integrity protection and origin authentication. CMC can encrypt requests, while CMP can rely on a lower-layer protocol such as TLS or IPsec.

A PGP User ID is an unrestricted octet string, while the request's Sender is an ASN.1 GeneralName, so comparing them is hard. An attacker could craft a User ID to get a certificate for someone else's identity. The RFC says it is safer for the CA to rebuild the User ID from the authenticated Sender name.

Supporting PGP means servers must also parse PGP streams, which could add vulnerabilities. It is recommended that the CMP or CMC servers run on a separate machine from the main CA, without access to the CA key or write access to the CA store.
sections.plainLanguage: Names on the new certificates are free-form, so a trickster could write a sneaky name. The issuer should write the name itself from what it already knows is true.
